entries.reason: Real-runner acceptance for the declared write boundary: four fixtures (vitest, jest, unittest, Playwright), each probed in a sandbox with a read-only and a writable copy of node_modules and a before/after listing, a few minutes in total. Mandatory in npm test and CI. The claims about the boundary (TG-SCRATCH-ROOT-IS-ONE-CALLS-DIRECTORY, TG-NODE-MODULES-IS-NEVER-WRITTEN-THROUGH and the others) are defended by the fast tests in test/scratch-dir.test.mjs and test/write-boundary.helpers.test.mjs; naming this file as a self-probe defender would re-run four runners for every fault.

Real-compiler acceptance for --typecheck on fixtures/known-answer-typescript (hand-verified expected.json): about a minute of nested probes with a real tsc and vitest. Mandatory in npm test and CI, where the fixture's dependencies are installed and a missing install fails loudly. The behavior is claimed by the fast defenders test/typecheck-*.test.mjs files (a stub typescript), named in TG-TYPECHECK-*; naming this file as a self-probe defender would pay for real nested probes on every fault.

Real-CLI acceptance for --require-assertion-kill: it probes a generated project several times (probe, --json, admit, --runner-cmd, legacy reuse), about a minute in total. Mandatory in npm test and CI. The claim TG-KILL-KIND-IS-RECORDED-FROM-ERROR-IDENTITY is defended by the fast pure tests in test/kill-kind.test.mjs; naming this file as a self-probe defender cost 2900 seconds of the gate's budget.

Real-runner acceptance for the kill kind: six runners, each a small generated project probed three times (about a minute in total). It is mandatory in npm test and CI. The claim TG-KILL-KIND-IS-RECORDED-FROM-ERROR-IDENTITY names the fast unit and conformance defenders instead; naming this file as a self-probe defender would re-run all six runners for every fault.

Independent native Node acceptance oracle plus real CLI cancellation and restoration checks. Mandatory in npm test and CI; focused native report/controller claims retain their own mutation defenders. Naming this complete ten-fault acceptance fixture as a self-probe defender would repeatedly pay for unrelated nested probes, as with the existing known-answer fixture exception.
Argument parsing and dispatch only. Every behaviour it routes to is claimed where it lives (src/gate, src/status, src/probe, src/scaffold). Re-evaluate if logic moves here.
Thin command wrappers: read flags, call the module, print. The logic is claimed in the modules they call; the fixture CLI tests drive them end to end.
The bin shim imports src/cli.mjs and exits with its code; nothing to claim.
Text rendering of documents that are themselves validated; rendering carries no verdict logic.

Acceptance test for the Playwright fixture; it runs only where the fixture's own dependencies are installed (the CI playwright job) and is skipped elsewhere. Naming it as a self-claim defender would make that claim a false survivor in the main job. The fixture's expected.json is its oracle.

Acceptance oracle for the full known-answer pipeline. It remains mandatory in npm test and CI, but naming this 40-second fixture as a self-claim defender previously made two pure tree-safety faults cost 444 seconds. Pure claims use focused defenders; the fixture independently proves the composed pipeline.

Acceptance oracle for the sweep verb end to end: a real repository, a real change and a real runner. It remains mandatory in npm test and CI, but naming it as a self-claim defender would add roughly twenty seconds per fault to claims whose logic is already probed through focused unit defenders, and it would not detect the faults those claims carry. Same trade as test/probe.fixture.test.mjs.

The injected Python reporters. They are not JavaScript, so a claim here could only be probed by running TestGuard's Python runner against TestGuard itself — circular, and it would prove the runner with the runner. They are instead held to fixtures/known-answer-python, whose sixteen verdicts were verified by hand against `python -m unittest`'s own exit code and must reproduce under BOTH engines: any behaviour change in a reporter moves a verdict there, in CI, on every push. Re-evaluate if they gain logic the fixture cannot reach.

Build and release scripts that run only in CI and are proven by CI failing: the install smoke, the version sync (claimed as TG-RELEASE-SYNC-CHECK-FAILS-ON-DRIFT where its logic lives), the fixture verdict check, and the PDF build (its --require-chrome and page-count guards are claimed as TG-BRIEF-PDF-MATCHES-ITS-SOURCE). None ships in the package.

Restated as TG-PROBE-NEVER-EDITS-THE-TREE-IT-MEASURES, with both faults carried over unchanged. The old statement promised that a probe "reproduces the known-answer fixture's verdicts exactly", and no fault in it ever falsified that half: F1 removes the restore and F2 forces in-place isolation, which are both about tree safety. A claim that is defended and still over-promises is the one thing a probe cannot catch, so the statement was narrowed to what its faults actually prove. The fixture oracle is still run on every `npm test` and in CI; it is no longer the defender of a claim whose cost it dominated (444 s, 31% of the gate) for two faults a 4 s test set kills.

Replaced by TG-CALIBRATION-COUNTS-NOCOVER-AS-A-MISS, which states the opposite of one half of it. The old statement said nocover "carries no information about detection" and its one fault (every verdict enters the denominator) was killed — but the claim it defended was wrong: nocover is a successful measurement with the worst result, and excluding it scored a project with no tests for a subsystem better than one with weak tests, because its worst outcomes left the denominator before the ratio was taken. The other half (flaky and unverifiable are failed measurements and enter neither side) is carried into the new claim's statement and test. Not a rename, because the statement had to change; not a silent removal, because this entry says why.

End-to-end acceptance of `testguard admit` on the known-answer fixture (seven tests, 12 s locally and 17-22 s in CI). The claims it defends were found by probing every claim with a fault in src/admit or src/commands/admit with this file as the only defender: it kills TG-ADMIT-NEEDS-ALL-KILLED/F1 and TG-REPEATED-CLAIMS-ARE-ALL-PROBED/F6, and nothing else. Both are defended by fast files (test/admit-decision.test.mjs, which now also holds the decision's rules this file used to carry, and test/claim-options.test.mjs). Naming this file as a defender would run it six times per fault, 100 to 130 s against the 100 s per-claim ceiling, for no kill the fast files do not already make, which is the cost the 67-87 s TG-ADMIT-NEEDS-ALL-KILLED history is about. It stays mandatory in npm test and CI. The excuse still expires so a later edit re-examines it.

Changed only to pin the fixture git options (FIXTURE_GIT from test/helpers/git.mjs) so the suite no longer depends on the machine's global git config; no assertion changed. It defended no claim before this change and defends none now. The excuse expires so the next real edit to this file states the claim it defends instead of riding on this one.

Acceptance oracle for the full known-answer Python probe (about 20 s a run, most of it one deliberately hung defender), under both the unittest and pytest engines. The claims it defends were found by probing every claim with a fault in src/probe/runners/python.mjs or src/probe/pyimports.mjs with this file as the only defender: it kills TG-PYTHON-COLLECTION-ERROR-NEVER-KILLS/F1 and TG-PYTHON-ATTRIBUTE-PATCH-IS-STILL-A-DEFENDER/F1. Both now name test/probe-python-claims.test.mjs, which probes just those two fixture claims in a second or two. Naming this file would repeat a 20 s probe six times per fault, 120 s against the 100 s per-claim ceiling. It stays mandatory in npm test and CI (the python job also runs it under pytest). The excuse still expires so a later edit re-examines it.

Wiring for the Jules routines: it reads the public pull request list, the claims file and --help, then prints what the policy decided. Every decision (queue cap, decline window, weekly rotation, target lists) is a pure function in .github/scripts/jules-policy.mjs, claimed as TG-JULES-TRIAGE-BOUNDS-THE-QUEUE and TG-JULES-MERGE-GATE-HOLDS-BY-DEFAULT. Maintenance tooling; not shipped in the package.

Acceptance for --partial-on-budget: it probes a generated four-claim project (serial, --fault-workers 3, a budget-capped hang, a reuse round trip, and the command in-process) with an injected clock, about twenty seconds in total. Mandatory in npm test and CI. The behavior it exercises is claimed where it lives and defended by fast pure tests: TG-PARTIAL-BUDGET-NEVER-REPORTS-UNMEASURED-AS-MEASURED, TG-NOT-REACHED-RECORD-IS-NEVER-REUSED, TG-COMMAND-BUDGET-EXPIRY-IS-TOLD-BY-IDENTITY-AND-A-CUT-RUN-IS-THE-DEADLINE and TG-EXHAUSTED-EVIDENCE-IS-CROSS-CHECKED name test/partial-budget.test.mjs and the conformance suite; naming this file would re-run all of it for every fault.

Fixture builder for test/probe-partial-budget.test.mjs, the slow acceptance test above: it builds a four-claim node:test project in a temporary git repository and asserts nothing. The claims that matter are defended by test/partial-budget.test.mjs and the conformance suite, which do not use it.
